title: When is a linear optimal power flow safe to dispatch from, and which cheap AC repair makes it safe?
lede: research programme on linear OPF dispatch feasibility on the PGLib-OPF benchmark: the DC dispatch overloads branches on all 11 congested cases; a trust-region successive linearisation of the AC power flow repairs 7 of 11 at the AC optimum's cost, and on 12 held-out angle-limited (SAD) cases the same rules with linearised angle rows repair 7 of 11 (angle-blind: 3); at the AC optimum's voltage schedule (an oracle). Without it, at the case file's 1.0 pu setpoints, the repair clears 2 of 11 API and 2 of 11 SAD cases and none meets voltage and Q limits; a repair that moves voltage setpoints with P, with a small margin inside every limit, is fully feasible on 28 of 34 cases from that start at 0.17 to 0.34 % mean cost above the AC optimum (tuned on those cases; held-out test next); analytic Jacobian sensitivities give the same counts (29 of 34) with 2 power flows per round, but the QP, not the power flows, sets the run time; an audit of all 347 QPs against Clarabel finds PIPS failing on 26 solvable elastic QPs, and with Clarabel the repair is fully feasible on 21 of 34 (31 with the voltage stage) about 5x faster; LPAC-C, the linear model with voltage and reactive power, run one-shot, is fully feasible on 0 of 34 and has no solution on 9 (7 SAD); on 244 load-perturbed copies (each bus x 0.9 to 1.1) the repair is fully feasible on 0.66 (95 % interval 0.52 to 0.79) and 0.91 with the voltage stage, matching the one-load-point counts, though 101 of 360 copies (71 of 120 congested) have no AC optimum; traced with 30 rounds instead of 10, the repair alone is fully feasible on 31 of 34 (late finishers +0.41 % over the AC optimum), its misses are mostly curvature on thermal and Q rows, and the programme's convergence bound as written is refuted (one case stalls at local infeasibility); on 24 held-out cases of 500 to 2,000 buses the frozen repair is never feasible within 10 rounds (0 of 12 scorable), refuting H2 as written, and feasible on 6 of 12 within 20 rounds, 8 of 12 with the voltage stage; on the six cases whose DC dispatch has no AC power flow the stall is a voltage-collapse fold (Jacobian smallest singular value down to 5 to 9 %), and repairing at the fold then walking up in load clears only case300 TYP (+0.83 %), none of the five RTE networks; that stall turned out to be the slack: PYPOWER's reference rule puts a 15 to 30 MW unit there, and with the reference at the largest unit the DC dispatch has a power flow on all five RTE networks and the frozen repair is fully feasible on 3 of 5 (+0.02 to +0.62 %); IPOPT under PYPOWER's AC OPF solves all 12 large cases PIPS cannot, within 0.005 % of PGLib; rerun under one protocol on all 24 held-out cases (largest-unit slack, IPOPT reactive stage, PGLib reference) the frozen repair is fully feasible on 10 of 24 within 20 rounds and 12 of 24 with the reactive stage (DC dispatch: 0), losing none of the earlier protocol's cases, at a mean +0.50 % over the optimum; five cases have no DC OPF solution.
summary: An open research programme (opened 2026-11-12, track 21) on whether the dispatch from a linear optimal power flow, the model markets clear energy with, is feasible once the AC physics is applied, and how many AC power flows a repair needs to make it so at the AC optimum's cost. Benchmark: PGLib-OPF v23.07 (typical, congested API and small-angle-difference SAD sets of 12 cases, 14 to 300 buses), solved with PYPOWER, whose AC optima match the library's published values within 0.005 %. So far (experiments in infra-dcopf): the plain DC dispatch overloads branches on all 11 API cases with an AC optimum; a trust-region successive linearisation (finite-difference loss factors and flow sensitivities, a QP, an elastic l1 fallback) repairs 7 of 11 at the optimum's cost, with rules set on those cases; on the 12 SAD cases, held out, the same rules plus linearised angle-difference rows repair 7 of the 11 with an AC optimum, while the angle-blind version repairs 3 and lands 6.5–17.6 % below the optimum's cost by breaking up to 16 angle limits. Milestone 3 (2026-11-12): without that oracle schedule, at PGLib's own 1.0 pu setpoints, the same repair clears thermal, slack and angle limits on 2 of 11 API and 2 of 11 SAD cases (6 and 7 with it), none of its dispatches meets voltage and Q limits, and an AC OPF over voltages only after it makes 16 of 34 cases fully feasible at a mean 0.8–4.3 % above the optimum's cost. Milestone 3b (2026-11-12): a successive linearisation over P and the generator voltage setpoints, with voltage and Q limits as linear rows, is fully feasible on only 5 of 34 cases as pre-registered (it stops within 0.1 % of the limits on 19); with a small margin inside every limit (a variant chosen after that result) it is fully feasible on 18 of 34, and on 28 of 34 with the voltage-only stage after it, at a mean 0.17–0.34 % above the AC optimum's cost; not yet tested on held-out cases. Milestone 2 (2026-11-13): the same sensitivities from the power-flow Jacobian (one sparse solve per round, matching central differences to 1.3×10−5) give 19 and 29 of 34, so the counts do not hang on finite-difference noise; the run time falls only 1.1× because the QP takes 98–99 % of it, and a finished repair's cost moves by up to 3.1 points with the derivative source, since the method stops at its first feasible round. Milestone 2b (2026-11-13): every QP the repair poses (347) re-solved by Clarabel as a referee: where PIPS reports a solution it is the right one (objectives agree within 10−6), but PIPS fails on 36 of 99 elastic QPs, 26 of them solvable; with Clarabel on every QP the repair is fully feasible on 21 of 34 (31 with the voltage-only stage), loses no case, and runs about 5× faster. Milestone 4a (2026-11-13): LPAC-C (Coffrin and Van Hentenryck 2014, PowerModels' conic form), solved once and run through one AC power flow, is fully feasible on 0 of 34 cases; it has no solution on 9 (7 of the 11 SAD cases; a second solver agrees on 8), and where it solves the AC power flow breaks Q limits on 21 of 25, with 376 of 1,000 generator voltage setpoints exactly on a bound. As a starting point for the repair it is about as good as the DC dispatch (17 against 15 fully feasible on the 25 cases it solves). On 244 load-perturbed copies (every bus’s load × 0.9 to 1.1, 10 seeds) the repair is fully feasible on 0.66 (95 % cluster bootstrap 0.52 to 0.79) and 0.91 with the voltage stage (0.83 to 0.97), its one-load-point verdict matches the copies’ majority on 30 of 34 cases, and it beats the voltage stage on the DC dispatch on 29 cases with no losses (P = 3.7e-9); 101 of 360 copies, 71 of 120 congested ones, have no AC optimum and are excluded. Milestone 7, empirical half (2026-11-13): traced round by round with a 30-round budget instead of 10, the repair alone is fully feasible on 31 of 34 cases (by round 20; 21 at 10 rounds), the ten late finishers at a mean +0.41 % over the AC optimum; 168 of 224 misses in rounds 1–10 are curvature failures (the step’s second-order error exceeds the margin, on thermal and Q rows), the one-step finishing condition holds on all 190 hard misses, and the convergence bound H4 as written is refuted (10× or more off on 25 of 31 finishers; case73 API stalls with a well-conditioned Jacobian at a point of local infeasibility). Limits: one AC solver, few congested copies with an AC optimum, no baseline yet from LPAC-W or optimised linearisations. Target: IEEE Transactions on Power Systems. Milestone 6 (2026-11-13): on the 24 held-out PGLib cases of 500 to 2,000 buses (12 scorable; PIPS has no AC optimum on 11), the frozen repair is fully feasible within 10 rounds on 0 of 12, refuting H2 as written; within a 20-round budget fixed beforehand on 6 of 12, and 8 of 12 with the voltage stage (DC dispatch with the same stage: 0), at a mean +0.66 % over the AC optimum. Past the loading limit (2026-11-14): on the six cases whose DC dispatch has no AC power flow, the power-flow Jacobian’s smallest singular value falls to 5 to 9 % of its no-load value where load continuation stalls, a saddle-node fold; repair-and-continue reaches a feasible point on case300 TYP (+0.83 %) and none of the five RTE cases. The slack, not the dispatch (2026-11-15): with the reference moved from PYPOWER’s choice (a 15 to 30 MW unit carrying 505 to 687 MW of losses) to the largest unit, the DC dispatch has an AC power flow on all five RTE networks and the frozen repair is fully feasible on 3 of 5 at +0.02 to +0.62 %; IPOPT swapped in under PYPOWER’s unchanged AC OPF solves all 12 large cases PIPS cannot, within 0.005 % of PGLib’s published objectives. Milestone 6 under one protocol (2026-11-15): on all 24 held-out cases, with the slack at the largest unit, IPOPT for the reactive stage and PGLib’s objective as reference, the frozen repair is fully feasible on 10 of 24 within 20 rounds and 12 of 24 with the reactive stage, against 0 of 24 for the DC dispatch, with no case lost against the earlier protocol; clean points cost a mean +0.50 % (one above +1 %), and five cases have no DC OPF solution. Convergence (milestone 7, theory half, 2026-11-17): if the power flow is smooth along each step and every hard QP is feasible, a step shorter than a curvature radius finishes the repair and the trust region is halved at most log2(box / radius) times (1 to 12 on the traces, 0 to 5 observed); most rounds (162 of 228 misses) are accepted cost-driven steps that no assumption bounds a priori, and logging the elastic QP's own penalty shows the case73 API stall is a local infeasibility of the repair's controls (voltage violation within 1.6 × 10−5 of stationary), while case118 API stalls on the acceptance test (worst versus summed overload); accepting on the penalty changes no verdict. Trust-box widening (2026-11-19 to 11-20): when the hard QP is empty, re-solving it at the smallest non-empty box fixes the emptiness but cycles; capping the widening at twice the current box (rule C) and trying it only before the first halving (rule P) removes the cycles, and rule P finishes 32 of 34 development and 11 of 19 held-out cases with none lost against the frozen repair (31 and 10); one held-out case suggested rule P. On 33 unused PGLib cases of 2,001 to 2,999 buses (complete: 23 reach the repair, the frozen repair finishes 9) rules C and P each finish 7, losing 2 frozen finishers and gaining none, both losses through a round-1 widening; they are 0.3 points cheaper where all finish. The frozen repair stays and the widening line is closed as a finisher rule. A cost phase after the first clean point (2026-11-23), fixed before each rule ran: ten hard QPs on the case's own costs with the frozen margins (rule CP) lower the mean gap to PGLib's AC optimum from +0.39 to +0.23 points on development and +0.58 to +0.51 held-out; capping every margin at its own slack (CS) frees empty QPs but lets more trials leave the clean set; using the cap only on a round whose margined QP is empty (CF) is never dearer than CP on any of 83 finishers and brings the gaps to +0.21 and +0.49, so it is adopted On the 33-case confirmation split (2026-11-24), the method of record (repair, reactive stage, CF) finishes 18 and CF lowers the cost of all 18, never dearer than CP (cheaper on 10, P = 0.002), to a mean +0.66 % and median +0.09 % over PGLib's AC optimum.
